Release: datasette-charts 0.2a0

 I introduced this new charting plugin for Datasette yesterday . Today it's gained integration with Datasette Agent , so now you can ask chat for a chart and it will create one for you using the same underlying chart suggestion and generation tools.

 Here's a demo video, recorded on agent.datasette.io where you can sign in with GitHub to try the plugin yourself:

 Download the video (MP4)

 I prompt Datasette Agent to "Use #stats to show sqlite-utils downloads over time as a chart" - where typing "#stats" opens a table search box. It shows me a chart inline in the chat, and when I click "Open in the chart builder" it opens the chart in a panel along with the table page. I use the table page to switch to a chart of "datasette", then when I ask the agent "what does the chart show?" it notices that I changed the content in the panel and describes the new Datasette chart to me.

 Here's a Markdown export of the chat from the video.

 Tags: datasette-agent , datasette , visualization

blogs.title: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
blogs.description: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model…
blogs.content:
GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer

GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this:

 In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count.

 This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said:

 Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality.

 GLM 5.4 is not (yet?) available as open weights. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API.

 It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model.

 I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up.

 Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one:

 I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4.

 It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look.

 I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark.

 Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , llm , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release , ai-in-china , glm

blogs.author: Jack Clark
blogs.description:

Chines…
blogs.content:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers.

 Subscribe now

 Chinese researchers optimize Huawei chips with a kernel improvement benchmark:
 …AscendGYM will help China do its own form of RSI…
 Researchers with the Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, a Chinese research organization, have built and released AscendGYM, “a kernel optimization benchmark for Ascend NPUs”. The purpose of AscendGYM is to make it easier to use AI to develop custom kernels for Ascend chips from Huawei – especially important given the export controls that prevent Chinese organizations from acquiring frontier Western semiconductors and forcing them onto Huawei.

 What AscendGYM does and contains: The goal is for AscendGYM to be the best way to evaluate the efficacy of AI-designed kernels as well as design new ones. The software is meant to help researchers answer this question: “Given a correct kernel implementation, can the specific agent further improve its performance for a target workload within an acceptable budget while preserving correctness?,” they write.
 “AscendGYM evaluates performance across multiple deployment cases, the best achievable performance for specific shapes and scenarios, and the optimization cost required to obtain these gains. Together, these dimensions characterize cross-case applicability, shape specialization, and optimization efficiency.”
 The software includes the AscendForge evaluation environment, which provides unified interfaces for “compilation, correctness checking, performance measurement, and feedback”.

 How well can AI models optimize Ascend chips? In tests, the single best model is Opus 5, followed by GPT-5.6, followed by GLM-5.3. They test out models in Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode; Claude Code yields the best absolute scores, and GLM does well in it, while GPT does well in Codex. Opus 5 is more token hungry and GPT-5.6 more token efficient.

 Why this matters – ingredients for Chinese RSI: For AI systems to be able to build themselves, they need to be able to develop and improve the software that is used for their own training and inference. Software like AscendGYM will be an essential ingredient for allowing China to rapidly improve the efficiency of its own compute substrates. The software will also have a bearing on export controls, where it provides a route to improve the performance of Chinese chips and close the gap with Western alternatives.
 Read more: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs (arXiv) .
 Get AscendGYM here : AscendGYM (GitHub) .

 ***

 Lawrence Livermore scientists test out if AI scientists can communicate uncertainty about experimental results:
 …Can AI systems be appropriately conservative?…
 “An agent that reports a confident wrong number is worse than one that reports honest uncertainty, because nobody downstream can tell the difference,” write researchers from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in a new paper that tests out how reliably AI systems can give accurate score ranges even when dealing with uncertainty.

 Testing for uncertainty: The paper introduces SciResearch-Eval, “an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator”. The novel part of this eval is that “an agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth”.

 What they studied: They give AI agents a common materials science task – measuring a material’s thermal properties by heating a sample and fitting a heat-conduction model to its temperature response.
 “An agent receives a sample of unknown material, a simulator of heat conduction through it, one heating experiment, and budgets: four more experiments it designs, compute for simulations and fits, and a cap on actions. It must report the sample’s conductivity, heat capacity and rear heat-transfer coefficient with 95% intervals, and predict a measurement it may not run,” they write. “Hidden from the agent, the simulator may be under-resolved, physically wrong (the real sample has temperature-dependent conductivity, a glued joint, front-face radiation, or heat loss through its sides), or adequate but fed uninformative data”.

 Results – only the most powerful frontier models can do this : “When the simulator is missing real physics, only GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 are reliable at default settings; the Claude 5.5 models recover only at their highest reasoning setting, and older and open-weight models not at all.”
 These models are able to do well by automatically trying to measure where the simulator is accurate and where it is less accurate then bases their estimates on that, making them more resilient to the different ways the simulator gets broken in experiments.

 Why this matters – real scientists are careful, and so are powerful models: Papers like this are further indications that we’re entering an era of AI-driven science. Though many of today’s models can assist in scientific experiments, as this paper shows only a couple of the powerful models at the frontier are able to operate with such appropriate autonomous skepticism and inherent attendance to the scientific method that they can deal with unanticipated breaks in their equipment. This is both an indication of the science advancement to come and a sign of how the most powerful models are exhibiting more and more of an ability to generalize and make themselves robust to perturbations in their environment.
 Read more: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents (arXiv) .
 Check out the leaderboard here (official site) .

 ***

 Stanford professors launch AI startup that wants to create a world where thousands of models define the frontier:
 …Noeri sees two well-regarded AI researchers enter the neolab game…
 Stanford profs Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin have launched Noeri, “a neolab to push the frontier of plural intelligence”. They have raised $110m and are relatively light on technical details, but their main vision is that they want to create a world where the frontier is defined by powerful models which rely on the proprietary data of distinct organizations. “Rather than one monolithic source of truth, we can nurture many small, specialized intelligences, each tuned to a place, a people or a problem,” they write.

 Further details: “At Noeri, we are building intelligence that learns proactively and continually. Most AI today is trained once and then frozen, while the world it serves keeps moving,” they write. “We close that gap with living systems that grow out of our own research. Our work on test-time training showed that learning on the job after deployment can unlock new capabilities and lead to new discoveries. Our work on self-distillation found that a model can become its own teacher, learning from each mistake and solving hard problems in far fewer attempts. And our work on agentic orchestration demonstrated that a small model conducting a team of other models and tools can outperform frontier models at a fraction of the cost.”

 Why this matters – the political economy of the singularity: Currently, the dominant AI models are massive pre-trained ones from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI and a tiny handful of other companies. What would it mean for the frontier to be instead defined by a broader set of actors? This is a core question inherent to the political economy of AI and startups like this show how some people are going to try and utilize technical approaches to make that different vision a reality.
 Read more in the announcement tweet from Yejin (Yejin Choi, X) .
 Check out the official site here (Noeri) .

 ***

 Chinese researchers build an air-to-air drone identification set:
 …A2A-UAV will help people add more visual intelligence to drones…
 Researchers with Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Hong Kong University of Science and Technology have developed and released A2A-UAV, “a multimodal dataset for air-to-air UAV detection and identification”. This kind of dataset has obvious civil and military applications and will be used to create better AI systems for autonomous onboard sensing on drones.

 What A2A-UAV consists of: 105,263 samples, split roughly equally across three different locations – a playground, a park, and a garden – and also split equally across day and night. “Each sample provides one RGB image and one panoramic image for annotation”, as well as thermal images, RF time-frequency images, a radar point cloud, and metadata. Bounding boxes are provided for the RGB and panoramic images, but not the other ones.
 One use case of this dataset could be to try and extend annotations to the other modalities: “Specifically, the bounding boxes can be transferred to the thermal images to support thermal UAV detection, and the radar points can be associated with the visual targets to support radar-based UAV localization,” the researchers write.
 The full dataset comprises 271 independently extractable .tar.gz archives with a total size of approximately 2.5 TB.

 How the data was collected : “The data were acquired by a UAV-mounted platform equipped with an RGB-thermal gimbal camera, a panoramic camera, an RF spectrum analyzer, and a millimeter-wave radar,” they write. The data includes 15 target drones from 13 commercial models, including three separately labeled DJI Mini 4 Pro units.

 Why this matters – fuel for the physical world: Datasets like this are the ingredients for making it easier for AI systems to operate robots and drones in the physical world. They also have potential dual use impacts, though my suspicion is that datasets like this are pretty irrelevant to militaries relative to the kinds of datasets that – and I’m speculating wildly here – might be being gathered in Ukraine right now given the extremely sophisticated drone-to-drone conflict there.
 Read more: A2A-UAV: A Multimodal Air-to-Air Dataset for UAV Detection and Identification (arXiv) .
 Get a sample of the data from Google Drive here (Google Drive) .
 The full dataset will ultimately be available via Baidu Netdisk with the extraction code A2AD (direct link, Baidu Netdisk) .

 ***

 Tech Tales:

 Machine architecture and the objectivity crisis of Machine Hermeneutics
 [Memoir from a primary Machine Hermeneutics investigator, 2033]

 “We shape our buildings; thereafter they shape us” – Winston Churchill, human politician, 1943.

 The building was a vast representation of the proposed Upgrade Device and we walked around it, our footsteps echoing as the sound bounced off its curving walls, eventually dimming in the face of the baroque crenellations that covered the edges of every surface. We humans, a small group of us, the best of our kind, needed to make sense of this building and explain the science it represented, and only then could it be used.

 As per the terms of the Sentience Accords, any novel machine-designed insight or equipment needed to be fully explainable by humans before the machines would be allowed to use it. In the early years, this so-called “conceptual verification” had mostly been a matter of time: machines performed science and delivered new insights to the world, then humans studied these insights and made sense of them, eventually generating human-readable explanations of the machine logic. Once this was complete, whatever insights or tools that had been created could be used.

 But as the machines grew more advanced and their science went further, the work became more arduous: machines would invent ideas, then use the...

Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise

 Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 8,176 new readers. Few fields have changed more under AI this past year than math. Now, a single Anthropic mathematician and Claude may have solved a problem even the top minds thought was years, if not decades, away.
 Levent Alpöge says they just proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old prime-number puzzle that carries a $1M Millennium Prize and has long been seen as math's most famous open problem. As with AI's other big math wins, not everyone is thrilled.

---
 In today’s AI rundown:
 Claude helps solve math's biggest open problem

 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

 Test Gemini 4 Neon on finding billing errors

 OpenAI opens its private AI scorecard to rivals

 LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

 ANTHROPIC, AI, & MATHEMATICS
 🧮   Claude helps solve math's biggest open problem
 Image source: Claude / The Rundown

 The Rundown: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge used Claude to crack the Riemann hypothesis, the 167-year-old question often ranked as math's biggest unsolved problem, after ~6 weeks of work, and checkers say it holds up, even as no human fully gets it yet.
 The details:
 First posed in 1859, the problem asks whether prime numbers follow a predictable pattern, and the Clay Institute put a $1M “Millennium” prize on solving it in 2000.

 Alpöge shared the proof only as 17M lines of machine-checkable math, writing that Claude “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

 The groups behind Lean, the computer language used for verification, certified it on Saturday, saying they have “full confidence” that Alpöge’s proof is correct.

 The Association for Human Mathematics criticized the proof as “little more than publicity” for AI labs, saying no human could reasonably understand it.

 A rival proof from Alessandro Masullo surfaced hours later, reportedly made without AI over nearly 12 years, though others quickly flagged problems in it.

 Why it matters: The Riemann hypothesis was a problem top mathematicians expected to take decades of new theory to solve, and Alpöge and Claude just blew past those estimates. This proof may not change daily life, but once that speed of progress spreads to fields like biology and drug design, the practical payoff will really start to show up.

 TOGETHER WITH GRANOLA
 📞  Walk into every call already prepared

 The Rundown: You’re two minutes out from a call and can’t remember what you discussed last time. Granola Briefs does the prep for you overnight, so you join with a few lines of context already waiting.
 With Briefs, you can:
 See who you’re meeting and what you discussed last time

 Catch up on recent company news before you join the call

 Trace every point back to its source when you need to dig deeper

 Try Granola free . Get 1 month off any paid plan with code THERUNDOWN.

 THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE
 💡  The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

 The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.
 Kenny, Head of Sales: After a good discovery call, my proposal used to take so long that the buyer's urgency faded and the details got fuzzy. This workflow fixes that. I record the call using Granola, have Claude pull out the buyer's own ask, and draft the proposal from that instead of from a rate card.
 Proposals built from the buyer's own words close faster than generic decks, and offering a smaller “yes” option turns “too expensive” into “let's test it.”
 Result: a proposal drafted in about 10 minutes, sent while the buyer is still engaged, with the deal history logged in the CRM.
 Shubham, Editor: My investments sit across several platforms, so I use Claude to bring them into one unified dashboard. Instead of logging in to each app, I can see every mutual fund and stock I hold in one place, along with what goes into each one every month and how often.
 Live holdings and company fundamentals come in through MCP connectors, so the numbers match my broker, and holdings from my other platforms appear in the same view. Claude fetches a short summary of each position and updates it daily. It sets up reminders for each SIP date, the 10% step-up every April, other amount changes, and when tax is payable.
 The result is one accurate view with no logging in to each app and no spreadsheet to update by hand. Claude does the fetching, organizing, and reminding, and I make the decisions.

 AI TRAINING
 🧠  Test Gemini 4 Neon on finding billing errors

 The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll put Google’s new Gemini 4 Neon to work on an everyday job: reading a year of electricity bills against your bank’s payment history to find why the bill jumped and what was billed wrong, then drafting the dispute email.
 Step-by-step:
 Download a year of electricity bills as PDFs and your bank’s payment history as a CSV. Delete every bank row that isn’t a payment to the utility

 Start a temporary chat in the Gemini app, choose Deeper analysis (4 Neon) from the model menu, and set Thinking level to High

 Attach both files and ask for a month-by-month table of usage, rate, and total, plus which month jumped and why

 Ask where each problem appears in the files: the PDF page and line, or the bank row. Check two or three of those spots yourself before you rely on them

 Ask for a short dispute email with every date and amount. Check it against the files, then send it to the utility

 Pro tip: Ask for the evidence before you act on an answer. A model that names the page, line, or row is easy to check, and only takes a minute.

 PRESENTED BY VANTA
 🔎  Spot your AI governance gaps

 The Rundown: Vanta’s AI governance assessment is a free, 10-minute benchmark built by Vanta’s security, compliance, and AI governance experts. With AI agents already outnumbering employees 79 to 1, see where your program stands across five domains and what to fix first.
 With the assessment, you will:
 Get your AI governance maturity score

 Tackle unapproved tools and unclear ownership

 Prepare for a formal readiness review

 Take the assessment .

 AI RESEARCH
 📋 OpenAI opens its private AI scorecard to rivals
 Image source: OpenAI

 The Rundown: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki just published the internal scores the company uses to track the raw intelligence of its AI since GPT-3.5, asking rival labs to agree on shared limits they'd hold until tools for monitoring AI catch up.
 The details:
 The metric, log-perplexity, measures how well an AI predicts the next token; lower scores indicate better predictions, and Pachocki says it tracks with AI's big jumps.

 Pachocki tied OpenAI's biggest new skills in cybersecurity and math to scores below 0.8, down from about 0.99 for the model behind the original ChatGPT.

 OAI also revealed an unreleased internal model at ~0.73, with Pachocki saying they should “expect further transformative capabilities” in the 0.68–0.7 range.

 Sam Altman called the post “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while,” saying agreeing on common limits “would be very wise.”

 Why it matters: This post packs in three reveals: another call for industry-wide “common limits” on progress, a first look at where OpenAI's next internal model stands, and a marker for where the next big jump in capabilities should land. Similar to METR's report on Anthropic, the data is showing that acceleration curves aren't slowing down.

 QUICK HITS

 COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY
 ▸ Dave built a school-email digest that fills the family calendar
 Today’s workflow comes from reader Dave Kay :
 “With three kids in school, I get dozens of emails every week: homework and assignment messages from teachers, updates from sports faculty, general notices from head teachers, and digests from the school's content platforms.
 I asked ChatGPT to read my emails every day. Each morning it emails me a daily summary. It creates events in my Google Calendar. On Sunday, it emails me a week-ahead summary.
 The result is that a quick look at one email gives me the entire week ahead, outstanding actions, and assignment due dates. I use AI for most things, but this is my killer life hack.”

blogs.name: Tomasz Tunguz
blogs.title: What Kind of Factory Will You Build?
blogs.description: Read on tomtunguz.com → Before AI, we wrote software line by line. After AI, the best engineering teams stopped writing code & started…
blogs.content:
Read on tomtunguz.com →
 Before AI, we wrote software line by line. After AI, the best engineering teams stopped writing code & started building software factories : systems that write, test, & ship the code for them.

 So why don’t other teams build factories?

 They are. On November 21, Notion published “A New Shape for Work” 1 & LangChain published “How to Build a Knowledge Factory” 2 . One is a manifesto, the other a build guide. Both describe the exact same four-step loop applied to company knowledge : context, agent, trace, curator.

 This is the plan for shipping a factory. 3

 Notion puts it bluntly :

 “This structure is among the most valuable IP any modern organization can have, because it defines the limit of what is possible for agents to do within that company.”

 LangChain frames the same loop from the other side :

 “The goal isn’t to document everything before agents can start working. It’s to build a system where doing the work reveals what knowledge is missing, & resolving those gaps makes future work better.”

 A software factory has four components. A shared context : the specs, docs & history an agent reads before it starts. An agent that runs the skills & specs to do the work. An execution trace that flags what shipped, what broke, & what it cost. A curator loop that reads the trace & rewrites the skills & specs for the next run.

 The last two steps compound. A prompt with a document attached is a one-off. The trace turns the work into data. The curator turns the data into a better system. That is the difference between a factory that improves every week & a workflow that stays flat.

 The loop is not a vendor’s idea. It is what the work looks like once an agent does most of it. A knowledge factory has the same four parts as a code factory. The context is the docs. The agent is the answer. The trace is the wrong answer. The curator is the fix.

 Once you see the loop, it generalizes everywhere. A marketing factory turns campaign performance into better copy. An online ads factory turns ROAS 4 traces into new creative. A sales pitch factory turns call transcripts into sharper decks.

 Satya Nadella described the same shift at Microsoft Ignite 5 :

 “The new company looks like there’s a founder. The founder has a token budget. Then the founder hires somebody. That person also comes in, & then they have a token budget, & they figure out how to add the tokens & the wages & then keep building.”

 Factories are still rare because a factory is an operations project, not a model purchase. Someone has to own the context, write the specs, read the traces & run the curator on a cadence. This is the reinvention of work : defining & operating the factory for each team.

 Different departments, identical architecture. The question is no longer whether AI can do the work : it is what kind of factory you will build.

---

 A New Shape for Work , Notion, Nov 21, 2026.  ↩︎

 How to build a knowledge factory , LangChain, Nov 21, 2026.  ↩︎

 Neither post includes a benchmark, a customer result, or independently verified outcome. Both are vendor arguments about architecture.  ↩︎

blogs.name: Stratechery
blogs.title: Amazon Earnings, The Chip Question, About Agents
blogs.author: Ben Thompson
blogs.description: Amazon makes the case they are not like other compute providers, even as they signal the willingness to give up margin to serve the frontier.
blogs.content:
Amazon makes the case they are not like other compute providers, even as they signal the willingness to give up margin to serve the frontier.

---

Listen to this Update in your podcast player

---

Good morning,

On last week’s episode of Sharp Tech , Andrew and I continue to discuss the Jensen Huang situation, why I think everyone is thinking about agentic commerce wrong, and why I love the iPhone Duo.

Then, on Sunday’s subscriber only mailbag , we discuss our decision to embrace video, whether disruption theory is still real, and the challenge of selling AI using worse AI.

This week is the Thanksgiving holiday; there will be an Update today and tomorrow only, and no Stratechery Interview. There will also be one Dithering episode on Tuesday, and a subscriber-only Sharp Tech on Wednesday.

On to the Update:

Amazon Earnings

It was, needless to say, a very busy November; so busy, in fact, that I am only just now getting to Amazon’s earnings, which dropped at the end of October. From Bloomberg :

Amazon.com Inc. shares dropped after the company reported greater capital spending than anticipated and the slowest growth in the core e-commerce business in three years. Amazon said it spent more than $77 billion on property and equipment in the third quarter, far more than analysts’ estimates, while pursuing its effort to build data centers and fulfill demand for artificial intelligence services. Third-quarter sales were lower than anticipated, rising 12% to $201.9 billion.

Revenue at the cloud unit, Amazon Web Services, accelerated for the sixth straight quarter. Online sales gained just 2% to $68.5 billion, the lowest increase since early 2023, when Amazon was still working through the post-pandemic slump in online retail. Advertising sales, a business closely tied to the e-commerce franchise, rose 11%, the slowest rate since Amazon began breaking out such results in 2020. The shares fell 4.4% to $233.10 as the markets opened in New York on Friday. The stock is up about 1% so far this year.

CEO Andy Jassy did not reassure investors on the earnings call about Amazon’s spending; in fact, he doubled down:

On the CapEx involved to grow the way we’re talking about, it’s meaningful. And I think that this — the way we think about it, Doug, is that this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. I think what we’re seeing with AI, it’s the biggest transformation in our lifetime. And if the idea of being able to grow 39% with $184 billion annual run rate and to grow 40% a year on top of that in each of the next 2 years and ultimately end up as $1 trillion-plus business, we’re going to invest to continue being the leader.

We are the leader today in the, I’ll call it, the infrastructure and AI space. And would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? Yes, it might be more convenient, but that’s not the world that we live in, and that’s not the opportunity. And we can fund this plan. And I think it will forever change the size of Amazon. It will forever change our revenue. It will forever change our free cash flow. And we’re going to invest and we’re going to pursue it to continue to be the significant leader like we are today.

The part that I thought was notable — and very much in line with a lot of the analysis I’ve been doing on Stratechery this year — was Jassy’s implicit assumption that AI compute is on its way to being a commodity business; this was in response to a question about workloads running on Bedrock, AWS’s managed inference service:

Well, you’re right that the majority and most of Bedrock today is being run on top of Trainium. And we do that in meaningful part because we really like the price performance that we’re getting, and it allows us to both keep prices as low as possible for customers as well as we like the margins associated with it.

If you think about margins in the cloud space and you’re looking at different players and what their cost structure looks like, there are a few things to pay attention to. The first is for their data centers, how many of them are they actually buying or long leasing versus doing colo or neoclouds. I mean neoclouds are about 3,500 basis points worse in operating margin than if you long lease them. And then you look at what is the hardware on top of which they’re running, and if you’re using the hardware that everybody else is using, you’ll have a comparable cost structure to what everybody is doing. And if you have the ability to use hardware that’s different, you’ll have an advantage.

And so I think when you look at what we’re doing, most of our capacity is either owned or long leased which enjoys better operating margins than what you’ll find when people are mostly doing colo or neo or a big chunk doing colo or neo. And the fact that we’re running on top of our own chip that’s providing both advantaged price performance and it’s more cost effective for ourselves because we own it, I think, gives us some structural cost advantages that I think are going to be very helpful to customers as we pass them back to customers and helpful to the overall economics of AWS.

This is the bull case not for a time when compute is scarce, but for when compute is abundant, which, incidentally, is exactly what investors are freaking out about right now. In a commodity market price is not based on differentiation but rather marginal willingness to pay: how much is the last entity willing to pay for a unit of compute? And, if we were to enter a scenario where there simply aren’t enough entities for all of the compute that is available, then the price will fall to the marginal cost of the compute that clears the market; everyone whose marginal cost exceeds that will simply not sell. Everyone who can’t make enough operating profit to pay for their debt load will go bankrupt.

However, that doesn’t mean there won’t be real money to be made in such a market; profit will be a function of having a superior cost structure, which is exactly what Jassy is claiming AWS will have. Moreover, the entities with the superior cost structures will be the last to lose demand, precisely because they will have the most capacity to handle lower prices (indeed, they will attract it, because they will be safe to build on).

Meanwhile, Jassy continued to make the case — reasonably, I think — that inference benefits AWS broadly:

We have a compelling flywheel spinning in AWS. Borrowing from Jim Collins’ flywheel definition Good to Great, where if you do A, you almost can’t help but do B and if you do B, you almost can’t help but do C and so on. In AWS, having the leading functionality, security and operational performance can’t help but drive customers to run their apps and store their data in AWS, which can’t help but drive AWS AI demand because customers prefer their production inference to be near the rest of their data and apps, which can’t help but drive core AWS demand because AI uses core for work like reinforcement learning, posttraining and tool usage, which can’t help but drive reinvestment back into our broader AWS functionality.

This is a different model than primarily hosting GPUs or renting short-term data center capacity. This is a long-term platform strategy that broadly helps customers invent and evolve their customer experiences, operate stably and build a reliable partnership they can grow for many years. And it also yields very attractive long-term economics for us regardless of supply scarcity.

Or, per the point above, regardless of supply abundance! In short, Jassy’s overarching point seemed to be, “We are not the neoclouds”, and he’s right!

---

Presented by

One way to tell if something has become valuable is that people try to steal it. AI startups saw attempted transaction fraud rates up to 4.3x higher than other startups, according to Stripe .

Then companies got better at stopping it, so fraud moved upstream. Fraudulent actors started creating multiple accounts to claim free trials and tokens. That abuse rose 40% in six months.

Stripe Radar is adapting accordingly, using signals across the Stripe network to identify abuse at registration and login, before a payment ever happens. You can learn more at stripe.com/radar . 

---

The Chip Question

Jassy confirmed that Amazon will be selling Trainium chips:

Customers using our custom silicon saved more than $2 billion in Q3 alone, and we just open-sourced TorchNeuron so developers can run existing PyTorch code, which most already use on Trainium without rewriting a thing. As we launch new generations of chips, demand for prior generations remained strong. After our launch of Graviton5, backlog for prior generation Graviton instances still more than doubled quarter-over-quarter. And short-term capacity for prior generation Trainium instances sell at a premium compared to the first half of the year. With Trainium demand so strong, customers continue encouraging us to make it available outside of AWS. We intend to do so late in 2027. Overall demand for AWS capacity remains exceptionally strong.

An analyst reasonably asked why, if inference demand is so strong, AWS wouldn’t just keep Trainium for itself; Jassy’s answer wasn’t very convincing:

On the balance of chips and what you sell externally versus what you use inside your cloud, it’s a very good question. And it’s a question that we’re continuing to evaluate as we speak. I would say that the number of companies who have a significant cloud business and a chip strong enough to sell externally is effectively two. So there really aren’t many customers that have to grapple with the same type of problem at this type of scale.

And at this point, everybody is producing their advanced chips with the same provider. There’s only so many chips that provider can provide each year. Everybody gets an allocation. And you have to decide with that allocation how much of it you want to sell externally and how much of it you want to use in your cloud. And there’s a trade-off. If you sell externally, you’re able to realize more revenue in the short term because you get to recognize the revenue as soon as it leaves your inventory. And on the flip side, if you decide to use it inside your cloud in the form of EC2 instances or Bedrock, you actually will end up driving more absolute revenue and free cash flow from those chips because you get to use them over 5 to 6 years and drive revenue for a longer period of time. So you have to really think through what you want to do.

To date, I would say that we’ve taken a different approach in how we’ve used our chips than the other provider who has the same type of balancing act going on. And as I mentioned earlier, we believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally, and we’re going to start in late 2027. And we will be thinking through that balance, I think, probably every year. But they’ll both be very significant. Our ability to create price performance, scalable chips is going to be a very significant strategic advantage for us at scale, both in our own cost structure as well as building a separate business and selling external chips and selling external chips really is a very different business than your cloud infrastructure business.

I admit, posting that entire answer was kind of a waste of time, but it’s always funny when executives clearly don’t want to answer a specific question. And some of the points were accurate! Only Amazon and Google make their own LLM accelerators at scale, and both are dependent on TSMC in the end, and have to make hard allocation decisions. And, critically, both have to make the same allocation decision, which, I strongly suspect, is “Do we want to keep Anthropic as a customer?”.

Anthropic and OpenAI are the two companies with sufficient demand to have leverage over Amazon (and Google), and, in the long run, they don’t want to pay Amazon and Google inference m...
